item.title: Study estimates 75% of NFL players who died over 15-year span had CTE
item.description: 258 points, 227 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (nbcnews.com)

→ HN comments  ·  258 points  ·  227 comments

Top #1 — cmiles8:

I would never let my child play contact football. The data is beyond clear that this sport causes irreparable life altering damage to the brain.

A lot of football players also suffer from mental health issues which, not to state the obvious, is likely not helped by banging your head all the time.

↳ reply 1 — chrisBob:

I am surprised by the otherwise intelligent and caring parents I have met who had their elementary schoolers playing tackle football. I don't understand that decision at all.

↳↳ reply — scoofy:

I grew up in Texas when football was basically religion. My parents flatly forbid me from playing. Any other sport was fine, no football. Every single person I knew on the team ended up with at least some kind of minimal, permanent injury. This was a decade before there were publications about CTE.

I'm quite thankful that I never ended up on the team, and think the entire concept of high school football is incredibly stupid given what we know about CTE.

↳ reply 2 — pton_xd:

I tried contact football in 7th grade and only lasted a few practice sessions. I was shocked by what I saw; other kids throwing their bodies into each other as if they were just bags of meat, sometimes colliding head-on. The ferocity with which they did it seemed like a source of pride for them and there was this sense of one-upmanship on who could tackle the best. The whole thing felt insane to me and I backed out immediately. I was involved in other sports like baseball and basketball so I was used to competitiveness, but nothing on that level of disregard for safety.

↳ reply 3 — pwthornton:

Play flag football. It's a great sport without the terrible risks. It's also being played by girls too.

I coach middle school girls. It's a blast. It has by far the most strategy of any youth sport.

If I had sons, I wouldn't let them play tackle football before high school, and I would have to think long and hard about that even.

I enjoyed flag football as a coach so much that I built my own play creation and team management software (https://getplaylook.com). One of the things that you get with flag at an early age because you aren't so focused on the physical side of the game is a higher emphasis on technique, particularly route running, and play design. Good play design can scheme people open, even if your team isn't very fast.

Top #2 — ggreer:

Here's a link to the study.[1] Since CTE can only be diagnosed by slicing up the brain, and former NFL players only tend to donate their brains to study if they're experiencing cognitive issues, there's obviously a bias in the sample. They tried to adjust for this by looking at rates of cognitive impairment in NFL players who donated their brains versus those who didn't. The ratio varied from 1.8x to 4x depending on age at death.

Unfortunately the number of brains studied isn't large enough to determine whether different positions have different levels of CTE. I'd guess that kickers would have very low risk compared to other positions, as they are rarely involved in collisions. Their stats hint that is the case, but the p-values are ridiculously high due to the small sample size.

1. https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle...

↳ reply — SkyPuncher:

This is good analysis. My only contribution is kickers CTE rates are likely correlated to CTE rates for soccer players. A lot of youth kickers are soccer players that decide to kick.

While soccer doesn’t tend to have as many concussion level impacts, there’s a lot of evidence that repeated sub-concussive impacts are just as bad.

↳↳ reply — ggreer:

I'd guess that CTE rates for football kickers are lower than for professional soccer players, as the rules forbid tackling or even running into them. A soccer player who becomes a football kicker will probably transition in high school at the latest. The total number of times they hit the ball with their head will be much lower than a career soccer player, and they'll stop doing it before players get stronger and kick the ball harder.

Kickers do kickoffs, extra points, and field goals. Besides that they're not on the field. The only time hitting a kicker is allowed is if it's some sort of fake play where the kicker ends up running with the ball. Even then, there tends to be a gentleman's agreement where teams won't rough up the opposing kicker, as doing so means their own kicker is fair game.

I knew one guy who was a kicker for a PAC-12 team (back when it was the PAC-10). He said he was hit only once in 4 years. Earlier in the game he'd insulted someone on the other team, and the next time they were both on the field, the guy hit him from behind long after the whistle blew. That's not really a football injury as much as it's a violent crime.

As far as I'm aware, no kicker has ever been found to have CTE (though the sample size for them is very small), and their concussion rates are much lower than average. I think the studies on kicker concussion rates overestimate how often they sustain head injuries, as they likely incorporate data from less competitive colleges and high schools where kickers also play other positions.

Top #3 — retrac:

Don't forget the hearing loss and tinnitus, too. Boxers and footballers tend to go deaf.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2014/07/140707134223.h...

> Leonetti recently spoke to retired players alongside EarQ at a meeting of the Chicago chapter of the NFL Players Association. When Leonetti asked how many players had experienced concussions during their career, they all raised their hands. When Leonetti asked how many have experienced hearing loss approximately 25 percent raised their hands. When he asked how many have tinnitus approximately 50 percent raised their hands.

item.title: AI is destroying my CS degree
item.description: 125 points, 117 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (lordtoots.bearblog.dev)

→ HN comments  ·  125 points  ·  117 comments

Top #1 — tcdent:

> It's been a huge learning curve.

I have been doing this professionally for over twenty years, and I still learn something every day. Over the past couple years, with AI augmentation, I learn even more, move faster and go deeper into the systems that I work on.

A CS degree was never going to provide you with all of the tools that you need for a successful career. It provided you with the basics to get your foot in the door.

AI is not replacing you or an education. AI is raising the bar of what you can comprehend and retain. From someone who is technically minded (and self-taught), all I have ever wanted is to keep learning.

↳ reply 1 — pantsforbirds:

> AI is not replacing you or an education. AI is raising the bar of what you can comprehend and retain. From someone who is technically minded (and self-taught), all I have ever wanted is to keep learning.

AI is, in my opinion, absolutely murdering the junior dev market. It's now much more efficient to pay for a senior or staff engineer and set them up with a subscription to claude or codex. I think things are going to remain fine for senior+ engineers, but I genuinely don't know what advice I'd give to graduating devs at this time.

↳↳ reply — reasonableklout:

Yep, and we have hard data on this: https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/08/ai-is-hitting-entry-level...

> Stanford researchers find the employment trends they identified for entry-level workers last year are persisting and expanding. Specifically, employment levels for workers ages 22 to 25 in the most “AI-exposed” occupations are now 19 percent below those of their peers in fields less exposed to AI disruption.

↳ reply 2 — wilkommen:

Many people in the tech world seem to espouse a great love for "always learning", but the way in which it is said always feels funny to me. Learn about what? When people say this, do they mean that they want to always be learning the next programming language, the next web framework, the next thick-client frontend web framework, the next python packaging CLI tool (pypi, virtualenv, uv ...), the next Linux distro? I'm tired of the churn. Most of these tools are not different enough from each other and don't have different enough use cases to be worth learning, but that's what a job in tech often seems to boil down to. You learn to do a basic set of tasks with one toolset, then once you get proficient, you swap all those tools out for another set of different tools that work completely differently but accomplish the same goal in a way that is not appreciably better or worse than the last set of tools. With AI, this will only get worse, as the cost for making new tools goes down. There seems to be a lot of churn just for the sake of churn.

↳ reply 3 — JaumeGreen:

> A CS degree was never going to provide you with all of the tools that you need for a successful career. It provided you with the basics to get your foot in the door.

Yes and no.

I concur that it was never about the tools, although I've seen plenty of people advocating it had a more "practical" approach, using the same tools as companies use, and in the same way.

On the other hand it's not only about the basics.

In there you can go at depth in aspects that you will have to fight to use, like proper engineering practices, and might only be vital on the later stages of your career. And I feel that those learnings, plus the possibility of acquiring a breadth of knowledge that is hardly possible otherwise, is what gives CS graduates a leg up to other practitioners of the art of software development.

YMMV and a leg up can be easily overtaken, yes.

Top #2 — dahart:

I’m hearing this more and more from both students and teachers. It seems like everyone in education is frustrated and can’t figure out how to use AI for education productively yet.

TBH I’m also thinking about how to use AI at work for learning. (My work environment is 100% all-in on AI.) Everyone can see and admit that AI coding is making us lazier and that it produces too much code to do old-style line by line reviews. Some people are using agent teams to churn out millions of lines of code where there’s zero hope of reviewing it. We don’t yet know how to keep quality high and complexity low while doing agent coding, we’re just having them write lots of tests and hoping that when things break they’re easy to fix. Agents should get better at broad architecture in the future, but they’re definitely not there yet.

> The amount of work involved has also tripled

This has to be one of the big ironies of using AI. I’ve heard this from other students too. The problem is that old-style assignments where the level of difficulty was hand-crafted is way way too easy for an LLM, therefore teachers need to crank the level of difficulty so the student has to actually spend some time on the assignment. But LLMs are getting better every month and the difficulty is so high that no students can possibly do the assignment by hand and now small errors in assignment design can lead to large errors in effort and time required.

↳ reply 1 — beej71:

> It seems like everyone in education is frustrated and can’t figure out how to use AI for education productively yet.

Oh, it's terrible. I'm a computer science instructor at a university (I have 20 years of industry experience prior) and it was already bad enough before trying to predict where the market was going to be 4 years in the future. But a year ago, it was tough to predict where the market was going to be in one month.

So yeah, we can teach all kinds of stuff. But is it the right stuff? With one month of visibility, who can tell?

But now I feel like it's settled down a little bit. And now I feel like I have more like 7 to 8 months of visibility. One thing that's helped is that we see the hiring differential between seniors and juniors. So now we can answer the question, what does the market want? It wants the expertise between junior and senior. And I'm confident it'll want that for at least the next 7-8 months.

Good luck cramming that into 4 years, though! I figure we have to try to bridge the gap as best we can. Eventually, seniors will become rare enough that the expense isn't worth it. It'll become better to hire cheaper most-qualified juniors.

There's still some seriously open-ended questions though. How much does coding matter, for example? If you ask senior devs who don't do any coding how much they rely on their coding expertise to make decisions, you'll get a zillion answers across the spectrum. This becomes even more true for senior devs who use AI for coding. Heck, ask 100 devs if it's important that you can even read code or not and see what comes out!

And then there's the question of how do you teach those systems level thinking skills? Historically, universities haven't taught those skills. You came out of the University with general problem solving skills in technology, and then at your job you were exposed to a small corner of the codebase to fix some bug. Gradually, over the years, you learn more and more of the codebase and become more and more senior. We have to get that into our curriculum. I'm working on that as we speak and will be working on that for the next several years, it looks like; even if my position vanishes, I'll keep attacking it—this is a tough problem that's fun to try to crack.

Anyway, I hope someday my forward visibility gets back up to 18 months. Won't that be amazing. I'd also like to buy some RAM. ;)

↳ reply 2 — visarga:

> We don’t yet know how to keep quality high and complexity low while doing agent coding, we’re just having them write lots of tests and hoping that when things break they’re easy to fix

Implement more versions with different languages, frameworks, libraries and AI agents. Then you can do differential execution for testing, which is easier than imagining testing scenarios from pure code. You can fuzz or use production data (shadow mode execution) to get notified early of divergences.

Keeping a population of diverse replicas might be the simplest way to derisk AI code. When 2 replicas diverge an agent can decide - was it a bug in one of them, or was the spec unclear? Either way, if you fix a bug or clarify the spec you come ahead.

A separate class of problems is related to intent divergence. For that my solution is to keep a full log of all user messages during the lifetime of the project. Even 10,000 messages collected over weeks and months can be read and summarized in a few minutes. That means you can check for intent divergence with agents, but you always start from the raw source (your human messages) not from intermediate summaries and diverged code.

Combining the 2 ideas would make each replica agent derive the user intent separately from the same log.

Top #3 — moomin:

Answers so far are assuming that this is complaining that their traditional CS course is not that useful for getting a job anymore.

That’s not what it’s about. It’s actually from someone who genuinely wants to learn for the sake of learning who’s talking about how AI is creating havoc in her studies.

↳ reply 1 — Aurornis:

This is a blog post where it’s easy to see which commenters did not read the blog before commenting.

The real villain in this story is the teaching staff. They need to get their act together and stop using generative AI for courseloads.

In other words, they need to do their job. The parts about AI mandates changing every 3 months reeks of an overly bureaucratic, admin-heavy structure where the students’ learning is a lower priority being performative about AI for your boss.

↳↳ reply — dieortin:

You don’t know what pressures the teaching staff is under.

↳↳↳ reply — Aurornis:

Neither do you, but either way that should not become their students' problem.

People have to do their jobs. Having AI generate slop and then sending it off to students or coworkers is not acceptable. It's not the students' problem to deal with things that may or may not be going on in the administration.

They're paying a lot of money to get an education and the university, as a whole, needs to do their job.

Saying that the teaching staff is under pressure excuses nothing. Students are paying for an education and it needs to be delivered at acceptable quality.

↳ reply 2 — hbn:

I would argue the job thing is more at risk and opportunity for learning is at an all time high. You've got 24/7 access to a very skilled personal tutor.

AI can teach you, you just have to put the effort in to tell it to teach you. In some contexts, I might want it to fire off a utility bash script and I have no interest in learning bash so I just run it and don't worry too much about the implementation. But if I'm getting it to help me write Java code for work, I review the output and ask it about parts that I don't understand. And it teaches me way better than the old way of reading dry/bad documentation.

It's what you make of it.

item.title: Kalshi and its co-founders face felony charges for violating Utah gambling laws
item.description: 462 points, 452 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (arstechnica.com)

Top #1 — karmickoala:

Somewhat related: did you know that you cannot disable GMail's GenAI features without disabling the traditional ML powered features, such as smart inbox, which predates LLMs? In this case, Google/Alphabet is conflating GenAI/LLMs with traditional machine learning, so you can't opt out of genai---which necessarily requires access to your data by the models---without deactivating the previous non-LLM powered features.

Which I get it, they indeed can use LLMs to improve the previous traditional ML pipeline. However I believe bundling these options together shouldn't be legal and I never expected Google to employ dark patterns like this. When I subscribed, these features were provided by traditional ML, perhaps some BERT-like encoder architecture at most, however now I cannot keep that previous functionality if I don't wish to grant LLMs access to my data.

↳ reply 1 — dwroberts:

I did this (disabled AI features) and lost smart inbox and it honestly improved the experience: it made me realise how much rubbish I was subscribed to that I never read, so I unsubbed and blocked tons of stuff, and now my inbox is clear again

↳↳↳ reply — NewJazz:

Cleaning up your email subscriptions is always a good decision IMO.

↳ reply 2 — 4chandaily:

It is absurd. I disabled Gemini for my organization, and Google in return disables tab completion in gmail entirely. They are practically demanding I find an alternative at this point.

↳ reply 3 — YeGoblynQueenne:

>> When I subscribed, these features were provided by traditional ML, perhaps some BERT-like encoder architecture at most, however now I cannot keep that previous functionality if I don't wish to grant LLMs access to my data.

Sorry for the sidetrack, but why is it so common to consider BERT something else than an LLM? It is one of the earliest LLMs so it's nowhere near the size of more recent ones, but even wikipedia classifies it as an LLM:

  Bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT)
  Original author Google AI
  Release October 31, 2018[1]
  Type 

    Large language model
    Transformer
    Foundation model

  License Apache 2.0
  Website arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805 
  Repository github.com/google-research/bert
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BERT_(language_model)

And in any case it's an autoregressively-trained Transformer, albeit encoder-only. If it's not an LLM, then what is it?

Top #2 — mawadev:

I'm confused, so google made websites indirectly unusable with all the advertisement incentives and then the AI summary came that usually just summarizes some reddit posts and now they subtly and indirectly block universities from using their entire search engine because unis block the AI part of search? item.title: There is no posttraining data commons
item.description: 125 points, 30 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (openathena.ai)

→ HN comments  ·  125 points  ·  30 comments

Top #1 — woctordho:

Distributed post training over the internet is much easier than distributed pretraining. What we need is just agent traces, from everyone's daily use. Hugging Face already supports uploading agent traces, see https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/agent-traces

We've been developing DataClaw to help everyone collect agent traces, see https://github.com/peteromallet/dataclaw . There are other similar efforts, such as in https://old.reddit.com/r/LocalLLaMA/comments/1u795pb/donate_...

The raw CoT is encrypted for closed source models, but there are plenty of ways to decrypt them. Even without CoT content, the tool calls and the length of CoT are already good signals for post training.

In China we use 'transition stations' to access GPT and Claude. They collect GBs of plain text agent traces every day, and the data eventually belong to the open source community. My estimation is that there are already 10-100 TB of agent traces freely on the internet for everyone to download.

↳ reply — david_shi:

The data itself is good, but what about anonymization? I doubt the average developer would want their raw traces hosted publicly on the Internet.

↳↳ reply — woctordho:

There are automatic anonymization filters in DataClaw, and other solutions such as Pi's export. But my bet is that the concept of privacy is going to change as AI consumes everyone's data.

Top #2 — mindwok:

A posttraining data commons and the infrastructure surrounding it is the next great open source project IMO, akin to Postgres or Linux.

The Marin project from Stanford (and I believe now ran by Openathena, the authors of this blog post) is really promising and cool: https://marin.community/

↳ reply — lukasschwab:

I was impressed by Marin's published evals policies: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9409

Precise and very clearly written.

Happy to answer any questions. We have a discord https://marin.community/

Interesting project, and I’m torn between whether it’s a good idea or not. But in any case, doesn’t something like an open post-trained trajectories corpus already exist with e.g. Poolside’s trajectories?: https://trajectories.poolside.ai/

↳ reply 1 — pdpi:

To me the second response reads more like PR-speak, like somebody who's been over-coached on how to talk to customers.

I find it strange that they'd have an AI-driven followup email days after the survey. If you're automating it, why the delay? "Delay the response so it seems more human" is way too cynical.

It's worth noting that OP is talking about Ocado, too. I've been a client of theirs for over ten years, and the number one reason why I keep buying from them is that their delivery drivers never feel super-hurried. They have lower quotas than drivers for other services, and they always have time for a little bit of banter. Compare that e.g. to Amazon Fresh drivers, who'll always just leave the groceries at the door and knock. They're already gone by the time I open the door.

I find it unlikely that they'd automate this sort of second-level customer support response while not squeezing the everliving shit out of their drivers.

↳ reply 2 — advisedwang:

One particular sentence reads particularly human to me:

> It is rare to get feedback that tells us exactly what is broken and how to fix it. AI doesn't remember from one conversation to another, so probably can't say how rare something like this is at Ocado (although admittedly it could learn that it's generally rare in fine tuning). I also expect AI to be trained not to compare feedback with other people's feedback.

↳ reply 3 — jamessb:

And also to pangram 4.1, which rates it as 100% AI Generated.
